An indirect loss, which is also called a consequential loss
explanation: A direct loss is the cost to repair the damaged property, while an indirect or consequential loss is the financial harm of losing the use of it, such as a hotel room or a rented apartment.

stem: The government-backed market of last resort for high-risk property includes building coverage during construction, but it can never write:
options: Farm risks or automobile risks
Liability coverage
A dwelling in a crowded neighborhood
A deteriorated building
explanation: This market of last resort always provides liability coverage and includes the risk of a building under construction, but farm and auto risks are outside it.

stem: Insurance that pays when a field yields less than expected because of a covered peril comes in two broad types:
options: Named peril and open peril crop forms
Yield coverage and price coverage
Hail insurance and multi-peril crop insurance
Government pools and producer pools
explanation: Crop coverage answers for a loss of yield and splits into hail insurance, which pays only for hail damage, and multi-peril crop insurance, which picks up the other perils.

stem: The five percent that the trees, shrubs and plants coverage adds is measured against which limit?
options: Coverage A, the dwelling limit
Coverage B, other structures
Coverage C, personal property
Coverage D, loss of use
explanation: The trees, shrubs and plants addition is a percentage of Coverage A, the dwelling limit, and no single plant pays more than five hundred dollars.
topic: Basis for the trees and plants addition

stem: Collapse is not a named peril in the form. What does that mean for the insured?
options: Every collapse is covered automatically
Collapse is covered only when wind is also present
Coverage applies only when the collapse follows a cause the form recognizes, such as the weight of contents or hidden decay
Collapse is covered only for other structures
explanation: Collapse is not a peril in its own right, so coverage applies when the collapse follows a peril insured against, the weight of people or property, or hidden insect and decay damage.
topic: Collapse is not a named peril

stem: Coverage E, personal liability, carries a minimum combined single limit of:
options: $25,000 per occurrence
$300,000 per occurrence
$1,000,000 per occurrence
$100,000 per occurrence
explanation: Coverage E personal liability carries a minimum combined single limit of one hundred thousand dollars per occurrence.

stem: Coverage E obliges the insurer to furnish a defense under which circumstances?
options: Only once a suit is shown to have merit
Even for a suit that turns out groundless, false or fraudulent
Only after the liability limits are exhausted
Only when the insured fronts the defense costs
explanation: The insurer funds the defense through counsel of its own choosing and must do so even when the suit proves groundless, false or fraudulent.

stem: At what point does the insurer's obligation to settle or defend come to an end?
options: As soon as the claim is reported
When the insured asks for a settlement
Once the occurrence's limit of liability has been exhausted
At the close of the policy period
explanation: The obligation to settle or defend stops when a judgment or settlement exhausts the limit of liability for that occurrence.
topic: Coverage E end of the duty to defend

stem: When does Coverage F, medical payments to others, pay?
options: Whether or not anyone was at fault
Only where the insured carries legal liability
Only once a court enters judgment
Only for people who live in the household
explanation: Medical payments to others covers necessary treatment whether or not fault exists, and it stays open for up to three years from the accident.

stem: Coverage F reaches expenses incurred how long after the accident?
options: One year
Two years
Five years
Three years
explanation: Medical payments are payable for expenses incurred or medically determined within three years from the date of the accident.

stem: Which people fall outside Coverage F?
options: A visitor hurt on the insured location with the owner's consent
The insured and ordinary household members, other than residence employees
A neighbor injured off the premises by an insured's conduct
Someone hurt by a residence employee working in the course of the job
explanation: Coverage F leaves out the insured and the regular residents of the household, though residence employees are still included.

stem: Which falls inside the definition of medical expenses for Coverage F?
options: Lost wages
Prosthetic devices and funeral services
Pain and suffering
Property repair costs
explanation: Medical expenses covers reasonable charges for medical, surgical, x-ray, dental, ambulance, hospital, professional nursing, prosthetic devices and funeral services.

stem: For an injury off the insured location, Coverage F applies when the injury:
options: Happens while the injured person is trespassing
Grows out of the insured's business
Results from a motor vehicle accident
Comes from an animal owned by or in the care of an insured
explanation: Off the insured location, Coverage F applies only when the injury grows out of a condition on the insured location, comes from an insured's activities, comes from a residence employee acting in the course of employment, or comes from an animal owned by or in the care of an insured.

stem: How do the Section II supplementary payments relate to the policy limits?
options: They sit on top of the liability limits
They come out of the liability limits
They begin only after the limits are exhausted
They are paid by the person making the claim
explanation: Every liability contract carries supplementary payments, also known as additional coverages, and they are paid in addition to the limits of liability rather than from inside them.

stem: Which item counts among the supplementary payments?
options: The deductible applied to a property loss
Repairing the insured's own automobile
A $250 bail bond premium when the insurer does not furnish the bond
The insured's everyday household bills
explanation: Supplementary payments cover the insurer's claim costs and costs taxed against the insured, a two hundred fifty dollar bail bond premium, appeal bond premiums, accrued and prejudgment interest, and reasonable expenses the insurer requests, including lost earnings of up to two hundred fifty dollars a day.

stem: Once a covered occurrence is reported, a liability insurer is bound by contract to:
options: Defend or settle the occurrence
Wait for a court judgment before doing anything
Cancel the policy at once
Repair the insured's own property
explanation: Liability duties run both ways: the insured reports the occurrence, and the insurer investigates and must defend or settle any covered occurrence.

stem: An insured who is served with a lawsuit over a covered occurrence must:
options: Settle the claim personally and bill the insurer
Wait until the trial date to tell the insurer
Forward the court summons and hearing notices to the insurer
Ignore the papers because the insurer is already on notice
explanation: The insured's liability duties include giving prompt notice, forwarding all court summonses and hearing notices, and assisting in the settlement.

stem: An insured admits fault in an argument and promises the injured person a cash payment. The liability insurer may:
options: Reimburse the insured automatically
Raise the policy limit to absorb it
Report it as a supplementary payment
Refuse the payment, because the insured may make no obligation or payment without the insurer's consent
explanation: The insured must assist in the settlement and may make no obligation or payment without the insurer's consent, so a private promise to pay can be refused.
topic: No payment without the insurer's consent

stem: Section II of a homeowners policy is made up of which two coverages?
options: Coverage C personal property and Coverage D loss of use
Coverage E personal liability and Coverage F medical payments to others
Coverage A dwelling and Coverage B other structures
Supplementary payments and loss assessment
explanation: Section II turns the homeowners policy into a liability policy: Coverage E, personal liability, and Coverage F, medical payments to others.

stem: Which statement about a deductible on Coverage E personal liability is correct?
options: A $250 deductible applies to each liability claim
The deductible equals the Coverage F medical limit
Liability coverage is written without a deductible
The deductible is subtracted from every defense payment
explanation: Liability coverage pays on behalf of the insured and is not written with a deductible, and medical payments under Coverage F carry none either.

stem: When an insured expects or intends the resulting harm, Sections E and F respond by:
options: Refusing it, though up to $1,000 of property damage from the deliberate act of a child under 13 is still covered
Answering it the same as any other occurrence
Paying it up to the Coverage E limit
Refusing it with no exceptions whatsoever
explanation: Expected or intended harm is refused, but there is a single carve-out: property damage of up to $1,000 caused by the deliberate act of a child under thirteen is covered.

stem: Vicarious liability for a minor's operation of a car, aircraft or watercraft is refused because:
options: A minor can never be held legally liable
Coverage F already answers for them
That refusal only concerns businesses
Those exposures belong with auto, aviation and boat coverage
explanation: The policy refuses vicarious liability for a minor's use of motor vehicles, aircraft and watercraft because those exposures are the business of auto, aviation and boat insurance.

stem: The business refusal in Sections E and F makes an exception for:
options: A full-time retail operation
A part-time or occasional self-employed activity of an insured who is under 21
A manufacturing plant
Professional services
explanation: The business refusal does not reach a part-time or occasional self-employed activity carried on by an insured who is under twenty-one.

stem: Which watercraft does Sections E and F coverage reach?
options: Every owned boat, whatever its size
Owned or rented boats with outboards of 25 HP or less, and sailboats of 26 feet or less
Boats with inboard engines of any horsepower
Sailboats of any length
explanation: Watercraft are refused except owned or rented boats with outboard motors of twenty-five horsepower or less and sailboats of twenty-six feet or less; rented boats with inboard or inboard-outdrive engines of fifty horsepower or less are also reached.

stem: A rented boat with an inboard or inboard-outdrive engine is reached by Sections E and F when its horsepower is:
options: 25 HP or less
100 HP or less
Any horsepower at all
50 HP or less
explanation: Rented boats with inboard or inboard-outdrive engines of fifty horsepower or less are also covered.

stem: Which motor vehicles survive the motor vehicle refusal?
options: Vehicles that service the residence, vehicles that serve the handicapped, a golf cart used for golf, and a battery toy for children under 7 that tops out at 5 mph
Any vehicle the insured happens to own
All off-road vehicles
Every vehicle kept on the insured location
explanation: The motor vehicle refusal does not reach a vehicle that services the insured's residence, a vehicle that serves the handicapped, a golf cart used to play golf, or a toy for a child under seven that runs on batteries and cannot top five miles per hour.

stem: Aircraft and hovercraft are refused by Sections E and F except for:
options: Aircraft rented for more than 30 days
Hovercraft used on private land
Models
Aircraft that seat fewer than four
explanation: The aircraft and hovercraft refusal applies to everything except models.

stem: The care, custody and control rule removes coverage for:
options: Property damage to property the insured owns, rents or uses
Bodily injury to a visitor
Damage to a neighbour's property
Medical payments to a delivery driver
explanation: Sections E and F refuse property damage to property owned by, rented to or used by an insured - the care, custody and control rule.

stem: Which claim falls under the controlled substance refusal?
options: A claim for a dog bite at the gate
A claim for a slip on an icy path
A claim that grows out of the use, sale, manufacture, delivery, transfer or possession of a controlled substance
A claim for a fence a guest knocked down
explanation: Sections E and F refuse the use, sale, manufacture, delivery, transfer or possession of a controlled substance.

stem: The additional coverages of Sections E and F, also called supplementary payments, appear in:
options: Homeowners policies alone
Commercial policies alone
Auto policies alone
Every liability contract
explanation: Sections E and F's additional coverages, known as supplementary payments, are found in every liability contract.

stem: A producer reviews an application and sees a prior arson conviction. That background is which kind of hazard?
options: A physical hazard
A moral hazard
A morale hazard
A legal hazard
explanation: Moral hazards reflect illegal activity by an insured or applicant - an arson conviction, a felony or substance abuse - and they can sway an underwriter's decision and the premium.

stem: A homeowner puts in a swimming pool, keeps two large dogs and runs a licensed day care downstairs. Those exposures are grouped as:
options: Physical hazards
Moral hazards
Legal hazards
Morale hazards
explanation: Legal hazards are actions or operations that raise the chance of lawsuits, and pools, dogs, trampolines and home day care services all belong to that group.

stem: A driver carries liability coverage only. After an at-fault crash, that policy answers for:
options: The damage to the other person's vehicle, not the insured's own car
Both vehicles in full
The insured's own car only
Neither vehicle, because fault cancels out
explanation: Liability insurance, also called casualty, is tied to negligent acts or omissions, so a liability-only auto policy covers the car the insured hit while the insured absorbs the damage to their own.
topic: Liability answers for the other party

stem: Along with the controlled substance refusal, Sections E and F also turn away claims that grow out of:
options: A dog bite at the front gate
A slip on an icy walkway
A guest struck by a falling branch
Passing on a communicable disease, or sexual molestation, corporal punishment or abuse by an insured
explanation: The refusal list also reaches lawsuits that grow out of passing on a communicable disease, sexual molestation, corporal punishment, and physical or mental abuse by an insured.

stem: Which exposure does the business refusal in Sections E and F also turn away?
options: A child injured on the insured's swing set
Supplying professional services
Medical payments to a delivery driver
A visitor's dog bite at the gate
explanation: Sections E and F refuse the business of an insured and, along with it, the supplying of professional services.

stem: The dwelling policy is best understood as:
options: A package policy, like a homeowners policy
A property policy, not a package policy
A liability-only policy
A commercial package policy
explanation: The dwelling policy is a property policy rather than a package policy, though personal liability can be added as an option.

stem: The dwelling policy is built mainly for:
options: Owner-occupied homes that already qualify for homeowners coverage
Farms
Commercial buildings
Dwellings that are rented out to others
explanation: The dwelling policy is designed mainly for dwellings rented to others, and it is also used for owner-occupied homes that cannot qualify for a homeowners policy.

stem: Which dwelling form values the dwelling at actual cash value with no coinsurance?
options: DP-1
DP-2
DP-3
MH-1
explanation: The DP-1 basic form values the dwelling at actual cash value with no coinsurance, while the DP-2 and DP-3 forms use replacement cost with an eighty percent coinsurance requirement.

stem: Which dwelling form offers no additional living expenses?
options: DP-2
DP-3
DP-1
Both DP-2 and DP-3
explanation: Additional living expenses are not available on the DP-1; the DP-2 and DP-3 add them as a twenty percent additional amount.

stem: On the DP-1, Fair Rental Value is a twenty percent extension capped at:
options: One twelfth of the extension each month
The full extension each month
Half the extension each month
Two percent of Coverage A each month
explanation: On the DP-1, fair rental value is a twenty percent extension limited to one twelfth of the extension each month, while the DP-2 and DP-3 answer for actual loss up to the limit.

stem: Every coverage on the dwelling policy carries a standard deductible of:
explanation: All dwelling policy coverages carry a two hundred fifty dollar standard deductible.

stem: Every dwelling policy leaves out theft of personal property unless:
options: The dwelling is owner occupied
Coverage A goes above $100,000
The insured switches to a homeowners policy
The broad theft endorsement is attached
explanation: Every dwelling policy leaves out theft of personal property, so the broad theft endorsement should be attached whenever the optional contents coverage is selected.

stem: The dwelling-under-construction endorsement sets the Coverage A limit to the estimated value at completion and prices the premium at:
options: 100 percent of the normal premium
65 percent of the normal premium for that value
50 percent of the normal premium
150 percent of the normal premium
explanation: For a dwelling under construction the Coverage A limit is the estimated value at completion, and the premium is sixty-five percent of the normal premium for that value.

stem: The farmowners livestock coverage form:
options: Answers only for animals in transit
Answers for breed-specific livestock diseases
Answers for animals on the premises that stray into a neighbour's field and are hurt or cause damage
Answers for vehicle damage to livestock
explanation: The livestock coverage form answers for animals on the premises that stray into a neighbour's field and are hurt or cause damage, as both property and liability coverage, and it turns away animals in transit, animals at sale barns and stockyards, breed-specific diseases, and vehicle damage.

stem: Farmowners personal liability picks up custom combining when the yearly receipts from that activity are:
options: Under $2,000
Under $10,000
Over $2,000
Any amount, with no limit
explanation: The farm policy answers for custom combining liability under personal liability when the receipts from such activity stay under $2,000 a year.

stem: Crop insurance is best described as:
options: A form of liability insurance
A federal life insurance program
A branch of workers compensation
A separate classification of insurance that is technically part of property insurance
explanation: Crop insurance is a separate classification that is technically a portion of property insurance, and it answers for loss of yield caused by a covered peril.

stem: A crop grower buys hail-only coverage. Which perils may be added to that hail policy?
options: Flood, wind and hail
Fire, lightning and transportation
Every peril that threatens the crop
None - a hail policy covers hail alone
explanation: Hail insurance answers only for hail damage, and fire, lightning and transportation extensions can be added to a hail policy; every other peril has to be handled by multi-peril crop insurance.

stem: Multi-peril crop insurance is sold and administered by private companies and is reinsured by:
options: The Kansas FAIR plan
The Federal Crop Insurance Corporation, an agency of the U.S. Department of Agriculture
The Kansas Property and Casualty Guaranty Association
The National Crop Insurance Services
explanation: Multi-peril crop insurance is sold and administered by private insurers and reinsured by the Federal Crop Insurance Corporation, an agency under the U.S. Department of Agriculture; the National Crop Insurance Services is the voluntary rate-making body.

stem: The Kansas plan that acts as a last resort for hard-to-place property will always provide:
options: Farm coverage as readily as dwelling coverage
Auto coverage for a high-risk driver
No liability coverage at all
Liability coverage, while it cannot write farm or auto risks
explanation: The Kansas FAIR plan serves high-risk residential and commercial property, includes builder's risk during construction and always provides liability, but it cannot cover farm or auto risks and does not write standard crime coverage.

stem: The dwelling policy will not accept a business on the premises except:
options: An incidental service business with two or fewer employees
A retail store with three clerks
A home day care with five children
Any business the owner happens to run alone
explanation: Farms and businesses are outside the dwelling program, apart from an incidental service business that has two or fewer employees.

stem: Every mobile homeowners form settles losses on which basis?
options: Replacement cost only
Agreed value only
Actual cash value only
Market value up to the limit
explanation: Every mobile homeowners form provides coverage on an actual cash value basis only.

stem: Which units fall outside the mobile homeowners program entirely?
options: Motor homes and camper trailers
Double-wide mobile homes that are tied down
Skirted mobile homes with the wheels taken off
Mobile homes resting on permanent foundations
explanation: The mobile homeowners forms are written for mobile homes only; motor homes and camper trailers never qualify, however they are placed.

stem: Before an MH policy will apply, the home has to be permanently placed and also:
options: Resting on concrete blocks by itself
Titled and registered as a vehicle
Skirted, anchored down with the wheels taken off
Occupied by its owner for a full year
explanation: To qualify, the home must be permanently placed, skirted, secured with tie-downs, and have its wheels taken off.

stem: An MH policy stops covering the mobile home when:
options: It stays vacant for 30 days
The wheels are removed
The base is skirted
It is transported or moved to a new location
explanation: The policy does not cover the mobile home while it is being transported or moved to a new location.

stem: A mobile home that cannot qualify for an MH policy might instead be written on:
options: An HO-5 comprehensive form
A DP-1 dwelling policy
A commercial package policy
An HO-4 contents broad form
explanation: A mobile home that cannot qualify for an MH policy can be covered by a DP-1 dwelling policy.

stem: How many mobile homeowners forms are there?
options: Two: MH-1 and MH-2
Four: MH-1 through MH-4
Three: MH-1, MH-2 and MH-3
One: MH-3
explanation: There are three forms - MH-1, MH-2 and MH-3 - and all of them provide coverage on an actual cash value basis only.

stem: Which of these describes mobile homeowners coverage accurately?
options: Losses settle at actual cash value, not the replacement cost basis that DP-2 and DP-3 use
Buildings settle at replacement cost, as on the DP-3 form
Values are agreed in advance, as with scheduled property
Buildings settle at replacement cost while contents settle at agreed value
explanation: The mobile homeowners forms always settle at actual cash value; the DP-2 and DP-3 dwelling forms, by contrast, settle the dwelling at replacement cost and require eighty percent coinsurance.

stem: A common memory aid for form numbering says:
options: Every form is special except the mobile home forms
Lower numbers are always broader than higher numbers
The number stands for the deductible amount
Even-numbered forms are broad and odd-numbered forms are special, apart from the high 8 and the low 1
explanation: The aid runs: if the form number is even the coverage is broad, if it is odd the coverage is special, apart from the high 8 and the low 1 - which matches homeowners forms such as HO-2 and HO-5.

stem: Which of these is a condition the MH program requires?
options: The home must be under five years old
The home must be tied down
The home must sit on a foundation
The home must be owner occupied
explanation: The MH program requires permanent location, skirting, tying the home down, and removing the wheels.

stem: A mobile home written on a DP-1 would settle a dwelling loss:
options: At replacement cost with 80 percent coinsurance
At actual cash value, with no coinsurance requirement
At agreed value with no deductible
At market value with no depreciation
explanation: The DP-1 settles the dwelling at actual cash value with no coinsurance, which is why it serves as the fallback for a mobile home that cannot qualify for the MH program.

stem: A mobile home owner in a participating Kansas community wants flood protection. Flood damage is:
options: Covered automatically by every dwelling form
Covered only on the MH-3 form
Covered by the FAIR plan instead
Not covered by a standard property policy, so a separate flood policy is needed
explanation: Flood is not a covered peril on a standard policy, so a separate National Flood Insurance Program policy is required, written through a participating community after a 30-day waiting period.

stem: A flood is defined as a general and temporary condition of partial or complete inundation of:
options: Two or more acres, or two or more properties, of normally dry land
Any single acre of land
Only the land inside a mapped flood zone
One property, if it belongs to the insured
explanation: A flood is the general and temporary partial or complete inundation of two or more acres, or two or more properties, of normally dry land, and mudflow is treated as part of flood as well.

stem: On the regular program of the National Flood Insurance Program, the most that can be insured is:
options: $35,000 on the dwelling and $10,000 on the contents
$100,000 on the dwelling and $250,000 on the contents
$250,000 on the dwelling and $100,000 on the contents
$500,000 on the dwelling and $500,000 on the contents
explanation: Regular-program limits are $250,000 for the dwelling and $100,000 for the contents; the emergency program is far lower at $35,000 and $10,000.

stem: A brand new personal-lines policy is just issued. The insurer may cancel it for any reason during the first:
options: 60 days
10 days
30 days
90 days
explanation: On a newly issued personal-lines policy the insurer may cancel for any reason in the first 60 days, and only for specified reasons afterward; the window is 90 days on a commercial policy.

stem: For property and casualty insurance, insurable interest must exist:
options: Only when the application is signed
When the policy is delivered
At the time of the loss
Continuously from application to loss
explanation: Property and casualty coverage calls for insurable interest at the time of loss, while life and health coverage requires it when the policy goes into effect.

stem: Workers compensation pays benefits to an injured worker:
options: Only when the employer acted negligently
Only when the worker bears no responsibility at all
Only after the worker files a lawsuit
Whether or not anyone was at fault
explanation: The whole point of workers compensation is to deliver benefits to injured workers regardless of fault or negligence.

stem: Which three employer defenses did workers compensation replace?
options: Comparative fault, strict liability, and absolute liability
Assumption of risk, contributory negligence, and the fellow servant rule
Subrogation, salvage, and liberalization
Estoppel, waiver, and arbitration
explanation: Workers compensation is a social remedy for the three defenses an employer once relied on: assumption of risk, contributory negligence, and the fellow servant rule.

stem: Which group is NOT required to carry workers compensation coverage?
options: Construction crews
Warehouse staff
Farm laborers
Retail sales clerks
explanation: Coverage is mandatory except for real estate brokers and salespersons, farm workers, domestic workers and homemakers, employers with payroll under $20,000, workers covered by federal law, and sole proprietors, partners and the self-employed.

stem: Coverage is optional for an employer whose annual payroll falls below:
explanation: An employer whose payroll is less than twenty thousand dollars is among the exceptions to mandatory coverage.

stem: Employers liability is provided by which part of the workers compensation policy?
options: Part I
Part III
Part V
Part II
explanation: Part I is statutory benefits, Part II is employers liability, Part III is other state's coverage, Part IV is the insured employer's duties, Part V is premiums, and Part VI is conditions.

stem: Under Part IV, which duty falls on the insured employer after a workplace injury?
options: Investigate and deny questionable claims
Arrange medical care, notify the insurer, and cooperate with its investigation
Publish the state benefit schedule
Pay the state fund directly
explanation: Part IV places three duties on the insured employer: provide medical services, report the injury, and cooperate with the insurer.

stem: A monopolistic workers compensation state is one where:
options: Private carriers compete and no state fund exists
Employers must buy their coverage from a single state fund
Coverage is entirely optional for employers
The federal government writes every policy
explanation: In a monopolistic state, employers must purchase workers compensation coverage from the state fund; in a competitive state they may choose between the state fund and private insurers.

stem: An experience modification on a workers compensation policy:
options: Raises the premium when losses run below average
Leaves the premium unchanged
Applies only to farm risks
Lowers the premium when the employer's losses run below average
explanation: An experience modification reduces premium when loss history is better than average, while a surcharge increases it when losses are worse than average.

stem: Workers compensation rates are expressed as:
options: A rate per $100 of payroll for each job classification
A flat charge per employee
A percentage of the employer's gross receipts
A fee based on the number of vehicles owned
explanation: Rates are quoted per one hundred dollars of payroll for each job classification, and the policy is later audited.

stem: An employer that fails to provide required workers compensation coverage:
options: Faces no penalty when the injury was the worker's fault
Has the state pay the claim with no consequence to the employer
Owes a benefit equal to what the policy would have paid, commits a misdemeanor, and faces higher employee benefits as a penalty
Leaves the injured worker with no benefits at all
explanation: Without required coverage, the worker still receives what the policy would have paid, the employer is charged with a misdemeanor and fined, and the worker's benefits are increased as an added penalty.

stem: A Kansas workers compensation insurer becomes insolvent. Which organization stands behind the covered claims?
options: The Kansas Property & Casualty Guaranty Association
The employer's own loss reserve
The Kansas general revenue fund
The state workers compensation court
explanation: The Kansas Property & Casualty Guaranty Association answers covered claims when a member insurer is insolvent.

stem: How does the Kansas guaranty association treat workers compensation claims?
options: It caps every claim at $300,000
It excludes them entirely
It pays them without a dollar cap
It caps them at $100,000
explanation: Workers compensation claims are the one class the association pays with no maximum limit.

stem: Membership in the Kansas Property & Casualty Guaranty Association is:
options: Optional for each insurer
Limited to life and health insurers
Open only to auto writers
Required of every insurer holding a certificate of authority in the state
explanation: Every company holding a certificate of authority to do business in Kansas must belong to and fund the association.

stem: How is a member insurer's share of the Kansas guaranty association funded?
options: By a flat annual fee of ten thousand dollars
By a pro-rata assessment of net written premiums, capped at two percent
By voluntary donations from insureds
By a charge on each claim filed
explanation: Members are assessed a pro-rata share of the previous year's net written premiums, with the assessment capped at two percent of that amount.

stem: Which part of the workers compensation policy extends the coverage to an injury that happens in another state?
options: Part I, statutory benefits
Part IV, the employer's duties
Part III, other states coverage
Part VI, conditions
explanation: Part III carries other states coverage so an injury outside Kansas can still be answered.

stem: Under Part One, the loss of time benefit carries:
options: A seven-day elimination period, with pay made retroactive after three weeks
A three-day elimination period paid immediately
A fourteen-day elimination period with no retroactive pay
No elimination period at all
explanation: The loss of time benefit has a seven-day elimination period and pays retroactively after three weeks.

stem: What figure applies to the permanent total disability benefit?
explanation: Permanent total disability is capped at $155,000, whereas temporary partial and temporary total disability are shown at $130,000.

stem: A scheduled permanent partial disability benefit of 66 2/3 percent of average weekly wage for 120 weeks is paid for:
options: Loss of one finger
Loss of one eye
Loss of hearing in both ears
Loss of one foot
explanation: The permanent partial disability example pays 66 2/3 percent of average weekly wage for 120 weeks for the loss of one eye.

stem: How are survivor's death benefits structured under Part One?
options: A $100,000 lump sum together with a $1,000 burial allowance
A $300,000 lump sum together with survivor income benefits and a $5,000 burial allowance
A $130,000 lump sum with no burial allowance
A $500,000 lump sum together with survivor income benefits
explanation: Survivor's death benefits combine a $300,000 lump sum, survivor income benefits for a widow and children up to age 18 (23 while still in school), and a $5,000 burial allowance.

stem: How long does a worker have to give notice of an accident, and of an illness?
options: 30 days for an accident, 60 days for an illness
7 days for an accident, 30 days for an illness
90 days for both
10 days for an accident, 90 days for an illness
explanation: A worker has 10 days to give notice of an accident, or 90 days to give notice of an illness diagnosis.

stem: Part Two, employers liability, answers:
options: Common law claims made against the employer
Statutory claims made against the employer
Claims brought by the employer's customers
Occupational disease claims only
explanation: Part One covers statutory claims against the employer, while Part Two covers common law claims against the employer.

stem: What is the basic liability limit for employers liability under Part Two?
options: $130,000, and it cannot be raised
$300,000, and it can be raised
$100,000, and it can be raised
$1,000,000, and it cannot be raised
explanation: Part Two employers liability starts from a basic limit of $100,000, which the insured is free to increase.

stem: Which loss falls outside Part Two, employers liability?
options: An injury that happens outside the United States and Canada
A third-party lawsuit brought against the insured
A disease that is not classified as an occupational disease
A suit by an employee who is not covered by the Compensation Act
explanation: Part Two leaves out punitive damages, injury to a worker hired in violation of law with the insured's knowledge, intentional injury, injury outside the U.S. and Canada, damages from discrimination, and obligations already placed by workers compensation law.

stem: Exclusive remedy means that, in exchange for covering work-related injury regardless of fault, the injured worker:
options: May still sue the employer in every case
Must sue the state fund instead
Gives up the right to sue the employer when the employer's negligence causes the harm
Keeps the right to sue only for intentional acts
explanation: Under exclusive remedy, the employer answers for work-related injury and disease no matter who was at fault, and the injured worker gives up the right to sue over the employer's negligence.

stem: Where no primary coverage applies at all, an umbrella still responds:
options: With no retention or deductible
Only after the primary limits are exhausted twice
Only for auto liability
After a self-insured retention, which is a deductible
explanation: Areas not covered by primary coverage are picked up by the umbrella after a self-insured retention, which acts as a deductible.

stem: Apart from workers compensation, the most the Kansas guaranty association will pay on a covered claim is:
explanation: The association pays a minimum claim of one hundred dollars and a maximum of three hundred thousand dollars, except for workers compensation, which has no cap.

stem: A producer presents the Kansas guaranty association as a selling point, suggesting that any claim an insurer fails to pay would still be covered. This is:
options: Allowed if the client signs a waiver
Allowed for commercial accounts only
A violation of the act
A required Kansas disclosure
explanation: It is a violation for a producer to use the association in a sales presentation where it is implied that benefits a company does not pay would be covered.

stem: What role does the Kansas Insurance Commissioner play in insurance rates?
options: The Commissioner approves rates but does not set them
The Commissioner sets every rate
The Commissioner has no role in rates
The Commissioner sets only workers compensation rates
explanation: The Commissioner's office reviews most rates so market competition stays reasonable, but it never sets a rate itself - the office approves them and keeps watch.

stem: Which statement about umbrella liability coverage is correct?
options: It replaces the underlying primary policies
It is written only on personal risks
It removes the primary limits entirely
There is no standard umbrella form
explanation: Umbrella liability is broad excess coverage placed above primary limits, and it has no standard form.

stem: The Kansas Property and Casualty Guaranty Association responds to covered claims when a member insurer is:
options: Late in sending a renewal notice
Insolvent and unable to pay its claims
Writing coverage outside the state
Charging rates the Commissioner has not approved
explanation: The association provides payment for covered claims when an insurer holding a certificate of authority becomes insolvent, which is why every such insurer must be a member.

stem: Professional liability protects an insured for:
options: Accidental damage to a client's property
Failing to perform the services they were hired for, or performing them below the appropriate standard of conduct
Employee injuries on the job
Damage to the insured's own equipment
explanation: Professional liability responds when an insured fails to perform the services they were hired for, or performs them below the appropriate standard of conduct.

stem: What kind of liability exposure does errors and omissions coverage address?
options: Exposures from owning a building
Exposures from operating a motor vehicle
Exposures from employing workers
Exposures rooted in professional knowledge, skill or advice
explanation: Errors and omissions responds to liability exposures that grow out of knowledge, skill or advice.

stem: Whom does the lawyers errors and omissions form cover without listing them?
options: Every member attorney of the firm, as a named insured
The senior partner only
Only the attorneys printed on the declarations page
The firm's clients
explanation: The lawyers errors and omissions form treats all member attorneys of the firm as named insureds automatically, with no need to name them.

stem: Directors and officers coverage defends against lawsuits from:
options: Customers, for defective products
Employees, for workplace injuries
Stockholders, for wrongful acts and decisions that cause them to lose money
Regulators, for tax violations
explanation: Directors and officers coverage defends against stockholder suits over wrongful acts and decisions that cause stockholders to lose money.

stem: Directors and officers coverage protects each director and officer:
options: Individually, while they are performing their duties
Only as a group, sharing a single limit
Only after they leave the company
Only if the corporation is insolvent
explanation: D&O covers wrongful acts and decisions that cost stockholders money and protects each director and officer individually while they perform their duties.

stem: Employment practices liability answers claims such as:
options: Defective products sold to customers
Vehicle accidents caused by employees
Wrongful termination, discrimination, and abuse of an employee based on race, gender or sexual orientation
Property damage to a customer's goods
explanation: Employment practices liability answers suits over wrongful termination, discrimination, and verbal, physical, mental or emotional abuse of an employee.

stem: What does a consent to settle clause require of the insurer on a medical malpractice policy?
options: It may settle any claim without informing the insured
It must obtain consent before the insured may hire a lawyer
It agrees to pay punitive damages
It must obtain the insured's consent before it settles a lawsuit
explanation: A consent to settle clause obliges the insurer to get the insured's agreement before it settles a claim.

stem: Data breach or cyber liability responds when a business:
options: Sees its website slow down during peak hours
Has personal information it collected leaked or hacked, causing a financial loss to its customers
Has an employee lose a company laptop
Has a supplier deliver late
explanation: Cyber liability responds when the information a business collected is breached and causes a financial loss to its customers.

stem: In a bond, the party who collects when the obligor-principal defaults is the:
options: Surety-guarantor
Obligor-principal
Obligee-insured
Claimant
explanation: The obligee-insured collects on the bond when the obligor-principal defaults, and is the party the bond protects.

stem: Fidelity bonds are arranged and paid for by the ____, while surety bonds are arranged and paid for by the ____.
options: Obligee-insured; obligor-principal
Obligor-principal; obligee-insured
Surety-guarantor; obligee-insured
Obligee-insured; surety-guarantor
explanation: Fidelity bonds are arranged and paid for by the obligee-insured, and surety bonds are arranged and paid for by the obligor-principal.

stem: In Kansas, which party gives a producer the authority to write business for a particular insurer?
options: The Commissioner, by issuing the license
The client, by signing the application
The state exam administrator
The insurer, by appointing and certifying the producer
explanation: The state issues the license, but before it takes effect the producer must be appointed and certified by the insurer, which grants the authority to transact business for that company.

stem: Which of these is a separate class of insurance license in Kansas alongside property and casualty?
options: Umbrella
Bonds
Fidelity
Errors and omissions
explanation: Kansas licenses by class; alongside property and casualty the classes include life and health, crop, title, and bonds.

stem: After appointing a producer, how long does an insurer have to certify that appointment with the state?
options: 10 days
30 days
60 days
90 days
explanation: An insurer must certify the producer within thirty days of the appointment, and it is fined twenty-five dollars a day for failing to comply.

stem: Which party promises to pay the obligee if the obligor-principal fails to perform?
options: The obligee-insured
The obligor-principal
The Commissioner
The surety-guarantor
explanation: The surety-guarantor is the insurer that guarantees the obligee the obligor-principal will meet its obligation, and pays the penalty if it does not.

stem: A fidelity bond's discovery period gives the employer:
options: Two years to determine whether a former employee took money or property
Thirty days to report the dishonesty
Ninety days to file a proof of loss
No time at all once an employee leaves
explanation: The discovery period gives the business owner two years to determine whether a former employee took money or property.

stem: What does property damage liability cover?
options: Repairs to the insured's own vehicle
Injuries to the insured's passengers
Repairs to another person's car or other property the insured damages
The insured's own medical bills
explanation: Property damage liability pays to repair the other party's car or any other property of theirs that the insured hits with the vehicle.

stem: When the insured drives a car they do not own, their liability and physical damage coverage is:
options: Excess, because the coverage stays with the car
Primary, because coverage follows the driver
Void, since the car is not scheduled
Converted into medical payments
explanation: Coverage for a non-owned auto is excess, because the insurance travels with the vehicle rather than the driver.

stem: Which vehicle counts as a covered auto on the personal auto policy?
options: A three-wheeled vehicle
A 26,000-pound commercial truck
A pick-up or van under 10,000 pounds with four or more wheels
A farm tractor
explanation: Covered autos take in private passenger autos and pick-ups or vans under 10,000 pounds with four wheels or more; farm use is permitted as well.

stem: A newly added vehicle receives how much automatic collision and other than collision coverage when no other insured vehicle already has it?
options: 14 days with no deductible
30 days with a $250 deductible
None at all
4 days, with a $500 deductible
explanation: An added vehicle gets fourteen days of automatic coverage for what the insured already carries, but only four days of collision and other than collision when no existing vehicle has that coverage, subject to a $500 deductible.
topic: Automatic coverage for an added vehicle

stem: For a replacement vehicle, how long does Coverage D continue and how does liability behave?
options: 14 days to add or 30 days for Coverage D, with liability ending at 30 days
4 days to add it or 14 days to continue Coverage D, while liability runs to the end of the policy period without notice
No Coverage D days, and liability needs notification
30 days for both, with notification required
explanation: A replacement vehicle leaves four days to add it or fourteen days to continue Coverage D, and liability continues to the end of the policy period without notification.

stem: What is a temporary substitute?
options: A car rented for a vacation
An out-of-state relative's car
The vehicle driven while the regular car is being repaired
A newly purchased vehicle
explanation: A temporary substitute is the vehicle the insured uses while the regular car is under repair; a car leased for more than six months is insured as though owned.

stem: The named insured includes the spouse:
options: While living together and for 90 days after a separation or divorce
Only when listed on the declarations page
For a full year after a divorce
Under no circumstances
explanation: The named insured takes in the spouse while the two live together and for ninety days after a separation or divorce.

stem: Which of the following is excluded by the personal auto policy?
options: A resident-relative family member
A temporary substitute vehicle
A trailer owned by the insured
A non-owned auto furnished for the insured's regular use
explanation: Exclusions cover intentional acts, damage to property being transported, prearranged racing, and non-owned autos provided for the insured's regular use.

stem: The policy territory reaches Canada and Puerto Rico, but:
options: Mexican coverage needs only a phone call
There is no coverage in Mexico
Mexican coverage is automatic for 30 days
There is no coverage in Canada
explanation: The territory is the U.S., its territories and possessions, Puerto Rico and Canada; coverage stops at the Mexican border.

stem: Which set names the personal auto rating factors?
options: Age and gender only
Age, gender, territory, driving record, primary use, and marital status
Territory and vehicle value only
Credit score and home ownership only
explanation: The personal auto rating factors are age, gender, territory, driving record, primary use and marital status.

stem: A driver pays the first premium on a car bought yesterday, before the policy is issued. What does the binder do?
options: It gives nothing until the insurer mails the policy
It locks the driver into the insurer for a full year
It cancels coverage on the driver's other vehicles
It stands in for the policy and covers the car at once, before the policy itself is issued
explanation: A binder takes hold the moment it is given and protects the insured while the policy is being prepared; the policy's issue date is normally the day the binder took hold.
topic: Binder and the start of coverage

stem: On a new personal auto policy, how long may the insurer cancel for any reason before it is limited to specified reasons?
options: 60 days
10 days
30 days
90 days
explanation: On a new personal-lines policy the insurer may cancel for any reason during the first 60 days; afterward it may cancel only for reasons the policy lists. Commercial policies get 90 days.

stem: A Kansas insurer may use a consumer's credit information when it underwrites an auto risk. Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, the applicant must be told in writing that credit will be used:
options: Only if the policy is later declined
Within 30 days of the first claim
Within 3 days after the inspection report is requested
Never, because credit cannot be an underwriting factor
explanation: The Fair Credit Reporting Act requires written notice that credit will be used within 3 days after the inspection report is requested, and if coverage is declined for credit the insurer must give the reason and the credit reporting agency's name.

stem: How does the personal auto policy treat a vehicle leased for more than six months?
options: As if the insured owned it
As a non-owned auto
As a temporary substitute
As an unlisted vehicle with no coverage
explanation: A vehicle leased for longer than six months is treated as though the insured owned it, so it takes the same treatment as a listed car.

stem: Beyond the named insured, who counts as an insured under the personal auto policy?
options: Any licensed driver in the state
Only drivers named on the declarations page
Anyone driving the insured car with assumed permission, plus resident family members
Anyone who borrows the car for more than 14 days
explanation: Other insured persons include anyone using the insured car with assumed permission and resident family members such as a ward or foster child.

stem: Which split limits does Kansas require for auto liability?
explanation: Kansas requires 25/50/25 - $25,000 per person and $50,000 per occurrence for bodily injury, and $25,000 for property damage.

stem: Which supplementary payment appears under personal auto liability?
options: $600 a day for lost earnings
$250 premium on bail bonds
The insured's deductible
Repair cost for the insured's own car
explanation: Supplementary payments take in a $250 bail bond premium, appeal bond premiums, interest after judgment, $200 a day for lost earnings when attending trials or hearings at the company's request, and other reasonable expenses incurred at its request.

stem: PIP is best described as:
options: Fault-based liability coverage
Coverage only for the other driver's injuries
No fault insurance
A substitute for physical damage coverage
explanation: Personal injury protection is no fault insurance.

stem: What amount does PIP provide for medical bills, and what amount for rehabilitation?
options: $4,500 for each
$2,000 for each
$25,000 for each
$900 for each
explanation: PIP sets aside $4,500 for medical bills and $4,500 for rehabilitation, in addition to $2,000 for funeral expenses.

stem: What does the PIP disability income benefit pay?
options: 80 percent of income up to $500 per month for 6 months
100 percent of income up to $2,000 per month for 12 months
$25 per day for 365 days
100 percent of income up to $900 per month for up to 12 months
explanation: PIP pays disability income of 100 percent of wages up to $900 per month for as long as twelve months, paid bi-monthly, plus a $900 monthly survivor benefit for up to twelve months for a spouse and children under 18.

stem: Which person cannot collect under the insured's PIP?
options: A passenger who owns no vehicle
A family member or other passenger who owns a vehicle of their own
The insured
A family member who owns no vehicle
explanation: PIP is unavailable to a family member or other passenger who already owns a car, while those without a car of their own may collect.

stem: What does the PIP definition of occupying a car take in?
options: Being seated inside the car only
Being in, upon, entering, exiting, near, under or around the car
Being belted inside the car only
Being within 10 feet of the parked car only
explanation: Occupying reaches in, upon, in the act of getting in or out, near, under or around the vehicle.

stem: What does uninsured motorist coverage pay for?
options: Repairs to the insured's damaged vehicle
The other driver's medical expenses
The insured's collision deductible
Injuries to the insured caused by an uninsured driver, an insolvent insurer's driver, or a hit-and-run driver
explanation: Uninsured motorist covers the insured's own injuries when the at-fault driver has no coverage, an insurer that has failed, or flees the scene; it does not pay for vehicle damage.

stem: Kansas permits a suit for non-pecuniary injuries only once the threshold is met, meaning:
options: Over $2,000 in medical bills, damage to a weight bearing bone, or permanent disfigurement or disability
Any medical bill, whatever the amount
Only after a fatality
Only when the other driver is uninsured
explanation: In Kansas a person may not sue another party for non-pecuniary injuries unless the threshold is met: over $2,000 in medical bills, damage to a weight bearing bone, or permanent disfigurement or disability.

stem: How does physical damage coverage behave on the personal auto policy?
options: It settles at replacement cost with no deductible
It settles on an agreed value basis only
It settles at actual cash value and applies a deductible
It is required by Kansas law
explanation: Physical damage coverage is optional, settles losses at actual cash value, and carries a deductible.

stem: Kansas groups liability insurance with casualty insurance because it answers for:
options: Negligent acts or omissions that harm another party
Damage to the insured's own property
Lost business income after a covered peril
The insured's own injuries caused by an uninsured driver
explanation: Liability is casualty insurance, tied to negligent acts or omissions. A liability-only auto policy covers the other person's car, not the insured's own vehicle.

stem: After an insurer receives a completed proof of loss, Kansas requires notice of acceptance, denial, or the reason more time is needed within:
options: 10 days
30 days
15 days
60 days
explanation: The insurer has 15 days from receipt of the proof of loss to accept it, deny it, or explain why more time is needed, and it must pay within 30 days after the proof of loss or a final agreement.

stem: An insured who is clearly at fault wants to settle privately with the other driver. Under the liability policy, the insured:
options: May pay any amount and seek reimbursement later
Must settle only after a lawsuit is filed
May settle only when the other driver is uninsured
Must make no payment or obligation without the insurer's consent
explanation: Liability conditions require prompt notice, forwarding of court papers, assistance in settlement, and no payment or obligation without the insurer's consent.
topic: Insured's duty not to settle alone

stem: Which loss is handled as other than collision damage rather than collision?
options: Damage from hitting a guardrail
Damage from a collision with an animal
Damage from rolling the car
Damage from striking a parked car
explanation: Physical damage splits into collision and other than collision; collisions involving animals, theft, earthquake and flood are treated as other than collision.

stem: What does underinsured motorist coverage add to uninsured motorist coverage?
options: It repairs the insured's car after any collision
It replaces personal injury protection
It makes up the difference between the other driver's limits and the insured's own
It pays the other driver's medical bills
explanation: Uninsured motorist pays the insured's own injuries when the at-fault driver has no coverage or has fled; underinsured motorist makes up the gap between the other driver's limits and the insured's own, and the two limits must match.

stem: Among the nine business auto symbols, which one reaches the widest?
options: Symbol 1, any auto
Symbol 7, specifically described autos only
Symbol 9, non-owned autos only
Symbol 3, owned private passenger autos only
explanation: Symbol 1, any auto, is the broadest of the nine symbols; symbol 7, specifically described autos only, is the tightest.

stem: Which business auto symbol gives the least coverage?
options: Symbol 1, any auto
Symbol 8, hired autos only
Symbol 5, owned autos subject to no fault benefits
Symbol 7, specifically described autos only
explanation: Symbol 7, specifically described autos only, is the narrowest of the nine coverage symbols.

stem: When symbol 7 is used, a newly acquired auto has how much automatic coverage?
options: Until the end of the policy term
30 days
14 days
No automatic coverage
explanation: Newly acquired autos are covered automatically to the end of the policy term under symbols 1 through 6, but under symbol 7 a newly acquired auto has only 30 days.

stem: Which two symbols does Kansas require?
options: Symbol 1 and symbol 2
Symbol 5, owned autos subject to no fault benefits, and symbol 6, owned autos subject to the compulsory uninsured motorists law
Symbol 8 and symbol 9
Symbol 3 and symbol 4
explanation: Symbol 5, owned autos subject to no fault benefits, and symbol 6, owned autos subject to the compulsory uninsured motorists law, are the two required in Kansas.

stem: When does the business auto policy cover mobile equipment?
options: For physical damage at any time
Only when it is driven on a public road
Never
Only while a covered auto carries or tows it, and only for liability
explanation: Mobile equipment falls under the business auto policy only while a covered auto carries or tows it, and only for liability.

stem: Cleanup of pollutants being carried by a vehicle and not used in its operation is:
options: Not covered
Covered as a supplementary payment
Covered up to $25,000
Covered by the towing provision
explanation: Covered pollution cost or expense pays to clean up fluids used in operating a vehicle that spill in a covered accident, but pollutants being carried by a vehicle and not used in its operation are not covered.

stem: Towing coverage under business auto physical damage has a basic limit of:
options: $20 a day
explanation: Towing coverage pays towing and labor costs each time a private passenger class covered auto is disabled, with a basic limit of $25.

stem: Business auto extensions for transportation expenses provide:
options: $20 a day up to $600, starting 48 hours after a theft
$25 a day up to $250, starting 24 hours after a theft
$20 a day with no maximum, starting at once
$600 a day for the first week
explanation: Transportation expense extensions pay $20 a day up to a $600 maximum when a private passenger class covered auto is lost, and coverage begins 48 hours after theft.

stem: Garagekeepers coverage is:
options: Required coverage for any business owning vehicles
Liability coverage for injuries at a garage
Optional bailee coverage for damage to vehicles left in the business's custody for repair or service
Coverage for the garage building itself
explanation: Garagekeepers is optional bailee coverage for damage to vehicles left in a business's custody for repair or service, and it may respond on a primary or excess basis over the customer's own coverage.

stem: The garage liability service form, built for service stations, repair shops and parking garages, covers:
options: Owned autos only
Non-owned autos on an excess basis only
Customer vehicles for physical damage
Non-owned autos on a primary basis
explanation: The service form serves service stations, repair shops and parking garages and covers non-owned autos on a primary basis, while the dealers form covers owned and non-owned autos on a primary basis.

stem: A commercial customer needs fleet coverage to begin that afternoon. What may the producer do?
options: Issue a binder and then cancel it alone if the risk sours
Issue a binder for immediate temporary coverage, which only the insurer can cancel
Issue nothing until the policy itself is delivered
Issue a binder that runs for the whole policy term
explanation: A binder gives immediate, temporary evidence of coverage. The producer may issue it, but only the insurer can cancel it, and the policy term normally begins on the binder date.

stem: A business owner with a small watercraft worries about rising water. Under the flood program, which property is normally left out?
options: The building itself
Mudflow damage
Vehicles and watercraft
Contents stored above grade
explanation: Flood coverage leaves out currency, lawns, trees, shrubs, livestock, vehicles and fences, along with personal property in a basement, while mudflow is treated as flood.

stem: A business needs coverage for a risk that no authorized Kansas insurer will write. Which arrangement fits?
options: An excess lines broker placing it with a non-admitted carrier
A binder issued by the Insurance Commissioner
A Kansas FAIR plan policy written for auto risks
An endorsement added by an admitted carrier
explanation: Excess, or surplus, lines brokers place unusual coverage with non-admitted companies when authorized insurers will not write the risk. The FAIR plan cannot take on auto risks.

stem: A service station takes in a customer's car for repair. Which coverage answers if the car is damaged while in the shop?
options: Business auto physical damage on the customer's car
Covered pollution cost or expense
The business auto towing provision
Garagekeepers, the optional bailee coverage for vehicles in the business's custody
explanation: Garagekeepers is optional bailee coverage for damage to vehicles left in a business's custody for repair or service, and it may respond primary or excess over the customer's own policy.

stem: A lay-up warranty on a boat policy does which of the following?
options: Extends coverage to any operator with no deductible
Suspends certain coverage during a lay-up period, such as a winter haul-out
Guarantees replacement cost for the trailer
Adds medical payments for injuries away from the boat
explanation: Lay-up warranties are common where winters bite: they suspend certain coverage while the boat is laid up for the season.

stem: The businessowners policy is best described as:
options: A single-peril property policy for large firms
A packaged policy with few optional coverages for certain small and medium sized firms
A liability-only contract
A contract written only for financial institutions
explanation: The businessowners policy is a packaged contract with few optional coverages, aimed at certain small and medium sized firms, carrying one property form on an open peril basis.

stem: Which operation is INELIGIBLE for a businessowners policy?
options: An apartment building
A retail store
An office condominium
A restaurant
explanation: Ineligible operations include bars, grills and restaurants, condominium associations outside the office and residential classes, contractors, amusement operations, wholesalers, financial institutions, and auto dealers or repair shops.

stem: What is the maximum gross receipts figure allowed for a businessowners policy?
explanation: The size ceilings allow six stories, one hundred thousand square feet with no more than twenty-five thousand square feet for any one occupant, and gross receipts up to three million dollars.

stem: What are the height and area ceilings for a businessowners policy?
options: 3 stories and 50,000 square feet for any one occupant
10 stories and 250,000 square feet with no per-occupant limit
6 stories and 100,000 square feet, with no single occupant over 25,000 square feet
6 stories and 25,000 square feet in total
explanation: The ceilings are six stories, one hundred thousand square feet, no more than twenty-five thousand square feet for any one occupant, and three million dollars in gross receipts.

stem: Peak season coverage under the businessowners policy provides:
options: An automatic 25 percent increase during busy periods at no extra charge
A 10 percent increase that requires extra premium
Unlimited coverage during holidays
Coverage only for outdoor signs
explanation: Peak season coverage adds a twenty-five percent automatic increase during seasonal periods at no additional charge.

stem: Business income coverage under the businessowners policy is written as:
options: A limit equal to 12 months of gross receipts
A flat $1,000,000 limit
An unlimited amount that ends at the expected resumption date but never past 12 months
A limit of 30 percent of the building limit
explanation: Business income is an unlimited dollar amount that expires at the expected business continuation date but never more than twelve months.

stem: If a covered building sits vacant for more than 60 days, the policy:
options: Cancels all coverage
Leaves only wind and hail in force
Doubles the deductible
Drops theft, vandalism and sprinkler leakage and reduces every other loss by 15 percent
explanation: Vacancy past sixty days removes theft, vandalism and sprinkler leakage entirely and reduces all other losses by fifteen percent.

stem: The honesty clause in a businessowners reporting form:
options: Gives a premium credit for accurate reports
Cuts the payment by the same percentage the insured under-reported
Requires monthly audits
Removes the aggregate limit
explanation: The honesty clause penalizes under-reporting, and a loss payment is reduced by the same percentage that was under-reported.

stem: Extra expense coverage pays:
options: The cost to rebuild the building
Lost sales for the whole restoration period
Costs the business takes on when it temporarily moves because a covered peril damaged the building
Employee wages during a slowdown
explanation: Extra expense reimburses expenses a business incurs when it temporarily relocates to prevent loss of income because the building was damaged by a covered peril.

stem: At what figure does Section II write fire legal liability?
options: $300,000 per occurrence, as lawsuit protection
$100,000 per occurrence
$1,000,000 per occurrence
$25,000 per occurrence
explanation: Section II business liability carries fire legal liability at $300,000 per occurrence, framed as lawsuit protection.

stem: A Kansas insurer writing businessowners policies submits its rates to the Insurance Commissioner. What may the Commissioner do with those rates?
options: Set every rate the insurer will charge
Write new statutes to replace the filed rates
Waive the premium tax for the insurer's first year
Approve and monitor them, but never set them
explanation: In Kansas the Commissioner approves and monitors rates to promote reasonable price competition, but does not set them, and the Commissioner cannot make or change laws.

stem: Kansas collects a premium tax from insurers that write commercial coverage. At what rate is it collected, and where does it go?
options: 1 percent of premium, kept by the Insurance Department
2.5 percent of premium, sent to the Kansas State Treasurer
5 percent of premium, paid to the federal government
No premium tax is collected in Kansas
explanation: The Commissioner collects a 2.5 percent premium tax from insurers and forwards that money to the Kansas State Treasurer.

stem: Which statement about the Kansas Property and Casualty Guaranty Association is correct?
options: Membership is voluntary for insurers that write businessowners policies
Membership is required for every insurer holding a certificate of authority, funded by assessments capped at 2 percent of net written premiums
It pays every commercial claim in full with no maximum
A producer may advertise it as a guarantee that unpaid claims will be covered
explanation: Every insurer holding a certificate of authority in Kansas must belong to the association, which is funded by a pro-rata assessment of net written premiums from the previous year, capped at 2 percent.

stem: A commercial insurer must satisfy the Kansas Commissioner of Insurance about its solvency. What does that require?
options: An audit every year, with claims reserves held in real estate
An audit only after a complaint is filed, with reserves held in stocks
An audit once every ten years, with reserves held in any asset
Its books, records and reserves examined at least once in every five-year stretch, or whenever needed, with claims reserves held in cash
explanation: Each company files an audited financial statement by June 1, and the Commissioner must examine its books, records and reserves at least once in every five-year stretch, or whenever it is needed; claims reserves must be held in cash.

stem: Which of these is an optional coverage a businessowners policy may add?
options: Employee dishonesty, written as a fidelity bond
The open peril property form
Premises and operations liability
Business income coverage
explanation: Optional pieces of the businessowners policy include employee dishonesty, which is a fidelity bond, boiler and pressure vessel or mechanical breakdown, burglary robbery and theft, money and securities, and additional outdoor signage.

stem: Premises and operations coverage responds when injury or damage:
options: Occurs only inside the business premises
Comes only from products the business sells
Happens at the business or grows out of the type of business conducted
Appears only after the work is finished
explanation: Premises and operations covers bodily injury or property damage occurring at the place of business or arising from the type of business conducted.

stem: How do the advertising injury and personal injury coverages treat bodily injury and property damage?
options: They never pay for bodily injury or property damage
They pay for bodily injury but not property damage
They pay for property damage but not bodily injury
They pay for both bodily injury and property damage
explanation: Advertising injury and personal injury are offense coverages; they never respond to bodily injury or property damage.

stem: Which offense belongs to advertising injury instead of personal injury?
options: False arrest and imprisonment
Wrongful eviction from a room or dwelling
Infringement of title or slogan
Malicious prosecution
explanation: Advertising injury takes in misappropriation of advertising ideas or style plus infringement of title or slogan; personal injury covers wrongful entry or eviction and false arrest, detention, imprisonment and malicious prosecution.

stem: Fire legal liability pays for:
options: Every part of the building
Damage to the insured's own building
Damage from a fire that begins off the premises
Damage an insured causes by fire or explosion to the leased part of a building
explanation: Fire legal, or tenant liability, covers damage an insured causes to that part of any building leased or rented if it burns or explodes, with the remainder handled by premises liability.

stem: Medical payments to others under the commercial general liability form:
options: Pays only after the insured is found negligent
Pays others' medical bills whether or not the insured was negligent, for up to 1 year from the occurrence
Covers employees hurt on the job
Pays for 3 years after the occurrence
explanation: Medical payments to others pays others' medical bills regardless of negligence in order to discourage lawsuits, for a basic minimum limit payable up to one year from the occurrence.

stem: What falls outside product liability coverage?
options: Bodily injury a defective product causes
Property damage a defective product causes
Harm to the product itself and the cost of recalling it
Injury that happens away from the business premises
explanation: Product liability answers for bodily injury or property damage a defective product causes, but never for damage to the product itself or the expense of recalling it.

stem: For product liability to apply, harm must occur off the business premises, with an exception for:
options: Restaurants
Contractors
Wholesalers
Financial institutions
explanation: The harm must occur off the business premises except for restaurants, and the product must be under the customer's total control.

stem: When does completed operations coverage come into play?
options: While the work is still underway when the harm happens
When the harm happens on the insured's own premises
When the product remains in the insured's control
After the insured has finished the job and left the site, so the harm happens off premises
explanation: Completed operations picks up defective workmanship or design that causes harm after the insured finished the job and left the site; it is always an off-premises exposure.

stem: How does a claims made form time coverage?
options: The occurrence may fall anywhere while the claim must fall inside the policy period
The occurrence and the claim must both fall inside the policy period
The occurrence must fall inside the policy period while the claim may surface at any later time
Both the occurrence and the claim may fall anywhere in time
explanation: A claims made form requires the occurrence and the claim to fall within the policy period; an occurrence form instead lets the claim surface at any future time.

stem: On a claims made form, reporting occurrences inside the basic 60-day window opens:
options: A 5-year window for claims of any kind
A 5-year window for claims from those reported occurrences only
A 60-day window for those occurrences only
Unlimited time for those occurrences only
explanation: Reporting occurrences that took place during the policy period inside the sixty-day window opens a five-year window for claims arising from those reported occurrences only.

stem: An insurer facing a liability claim keeps refusing to pay even after liability has become reasonably clear. In Kansas this is:
options: A lawful exercise of the insurer's discretion
A valid ground to cancel the insured's policy
Permitted whenever the insured carries other insurance
An unfair claims settlement practice
explanation: Failing to be prompt, fair and equitable in settling a claim where liability has become reasonably clear is one of the unfair claims settlement practices barred in Kansas.

stem: Which of these is an unfair claims settlement practice by an insurer?
options: Refusing to pay a claim without conducting a reasonable investigation
Giving a prompt and reasonable explanation when a claim is denied
Investigating a loss before making a payment decision
Settling a claim promptly once liability is reasonably clear
explanation: Kansas lists refusing to pay a claim without a reasonable investigation, and failing to adopt standards for prompt investigation, among the unfair claims settlement practices.

stem: A commercial insured is sued and turns the suit over to its general liability insurer. Which duty does the insured owe the insurer?
options: Set the settlement amount on the insurer's behalf
Withhold the court summons from the insurer
Make no settlement or payment without the insurer's consent
Pay the claim first and seek reimbursement later
explanation: After a liability loss the insured must give prompt notice, forward every court summons and hearing notice, assist in settlement, and make no obligation or payment without the insurer's consent.

stem: A business keeps a swimming pool, a trampoline and a home day care. In insurance terms these are:
options: Legal hazards, because they invite lawsuits
Physical hazards, because of the condition of the property
Moral hazards, because they reflect illegal activity
Morale hazards, because they show indifference to loss
explanation: Legal hazards are actions or operations that increase the chance of a lawsuit, such as trampolines, dogs, pools and home day care services.

stem: On a claims made liability form, what does the retroactive date control?
options: The date the first claim must be reported
The date the policy automatically renews
How far back coverage reaches for occurrences that happened before the policy began
The date the extended reporting period ends
explanation: A retroactive date caps how far back a claims made form reaches for occurrences that predate the policy; on a claims made form the occurrence and the claim must both fall inside the policy period.

stem: The commercial package policy is best described as:
options: An identical form to the businessowners policy
A monoline liability contract
A contract limited to financial institutions
A customizable package policy built for larger businesses
explanation: The commercial package policy is a customizable package policy, not a package in the businessowners sense, and it is designed for larger businesses.

stem: In the commercial policy declarations, the first name listed carries:
options: No special duties at all
The first named insured duties
A reduced premium
The exclusive right to cancel
explanation: The declarations note that the first name listed carries the first named insured duties, and that insured may cancel, make changes, and receives the bill and any premium refund.

stem: Which coverage part includes valuable papers and records?
options: Commercial general liability
Commercial crime
Commercial inland marine
Commercial property builders risk
explanation: The commercial inland marine coverage part includes accounts receivable, commercial articles, contractor equipment floaters, electronic data processing, installation floaters, signs, and valuable papers and records.

stem: What coverage basis does inland marine almost always use?
options: A special form basis
A basic named peril basis
An actual cash value only basis
A claims made basis
explanation: Inland marine insures certain kinds of property and is nearly always written on a special form basis.

stem: Which property cannot be insured on inland marine paper?
options: Contractor equipment
Accounts receivable
Valuable papers
Real property and the contents of a building
explanation: Real property and the contents of a building cannot be insured with inland marine policies and forms, and business personal property is not covered once it sits more than one hundred feet from the premises.

stem: Bailee's customer coverage is designed for:
options: The business's own inventory
